findings.claim: `GetHashCollisionResistantEqualityComparer<T>` no longer throws for types it cannot protect; it now returns `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`. With `MessagePackSecurity.UntrustedData`, any key type that is not on the allow-list silently gets a non-collision-resistant comparer. Untrusted payloads can then mount hash-flooding DoS attacks against Dictionary/HashSet keys. The requirement does not ask for this change, and it reverses a recorded secure-by-default decision (L12).

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.GeneratedFormatterEdgeCaseTests.UntrustedData_HashCollisionResistantComparer_RejectsUnknownType. It calls `MessagePackSecurity.UntrustedData.GetEqualityComparer<CustomKey>()` and expects `TypeAccessException`. It passes on base and fails on head, because head returns `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`.

findings.claim: In the no-surrogate path the collector always builds contractless members from every public read-write member. It ignores attributes on T: `[DataContract]`/`[DataMember]`, `[MessagePackObject]`/`[Key]` and `[IgnoreMember]`/`[IgnoreDataMember]`. Example: a referenced `[DataContract]` type with an un-annotated public property `Secret` still has `Secret` serialized. A `[MessagePackObject]` type with int keys is written as a name-keyed map. This breaks the criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured'; L21 defers to the requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.GeneratedFormatterEdgeCaseTests.DataContractOnReferencedType_IsHonoured. It compiles ProjectA (a `[DataContract]` MyObject with `[DataMember] Included` and an unmarked `Secret`) into a metadata reference. It runs MessagePackGenerator on ProjectB with `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class MyObjectFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<ProjectA.MyObject>` and asserts the generated sources do not mention `Secret`. It fails on head.

findings.claim:
Two models are added unconditionally to `modelPerType` for the same data type in these cases:
- T is also collected by the TypeCollector, because T is declared in the same compilation with `[MessagePackObject]`.
- Two `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` classes target the same T.

Nothing dedupes or diagnoses this. Depending on how ObjectInfos are merged, the user-declared partial formatter is either dropped, leaving the user class without an implementation (CS0535), or registered twice in the resolver.

receipt_plan.detail: Read MessagePackGenerator.cs:60-76: the TypeCollector models and the generated-formatter models both go into `modelPerType` with no check for a matching DataType. Confirm by running the generator on a compilation with `[MessagePackObject] public class T { [Key(0)] public int A {get;set;} }` and `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class F : IMessagePackFormatter<T> {}`, then compiling the output.

findings.claim: `IsPartial` checks only the formatter class itself. A formatter nested inside a non-partial containing type, e.g. `class Outer { [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class F : IMessagePackFormatter<X> {} }`, passes validation. The template then re-emits the nesting as partial declarations, so the user gets a compiler error (CS0260) instead of MsgPack019.

receipt_plan.detail: Read `IsPartial` (it inspects only the formatter's own ClassDeclarationSyntax) together with FormatterTemplate's `EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces`, which wraps output in the formatter's containing types. Confirm with a generator run on a nested formatter inside a non-partial outer class and compile the result.
